lesson.title: Drawing Power: The Power Triangle and Why Utilities Charge for a Bad Angle
lesson.summary: The power triangle plots real power, reactive power, and apparent power as the legs and hypotenuse of a right triangle, making the tradeoffs behind power factor visible and motivating why utilities penalize poor power factor.
lesson.body:
The three power quantities established so far, real power P, reactive power Q, and apparent power S, form a right triangle in exactly the same shape as the impedance triangle: P runs along the horizontal leg, in watts, Q runs along the vertical leg, in VAR, and S is the hypotenuse, in VA, with |S| = sqrt(P^2 + Q^2). The angle between P and S is the same power factor angle theta that showed up in impedance and complex power, and cos(theta) = P/S is the power factor itself. It is the identical geometry as R, X, and Z, just relabeled in power units instead of ohms, because power triangle values are simply the impedance triangle values scaled by the square of the RMS current.

Picking up the numbers from the complex power example, P = 1152 W and Q = 864 VAR for a load with impedance angle 36.87 degrees. The hypotenuse should reproduce the apparent power found earlier: |S| = sqrt(1152^2 + 864^2) = sqrt(1,327,104 + 746,496) = sqrt(2,073,600) = 1440 VA, matching the 1440 VA computed directly from V and I. The power factor is P/S = 1152/1440 = 0.8, and arccos(0.8) = 36.87 degrees, consistent with the load's impedance angle throughout every example that has used this same load.

This triangle is not just an abstraction, it is the exact tradeoff utilities bill customers for. Generators, transformers, and transmission lines are limited by how much current they can carry, and current is proportional to apparent power |S|, not to the real power P that the customer actually uses. A low power factor means a large Q relative to P, which inflates |S| and therefore the current needed to deliver a fixed amount of useful power. That extra current does real damage: transmission losses scale with the square of current, so a plant with a poor power factor forces the utility to push more current through its lines, and waste more energy as heat, just to deliver the same watts of useful work.

The standard fix is power factor correction: install a capacitor bank in parallel with the inductive load to supply reactive power of the opposite sign, canceling most or all of the inductive Q. Suppose a capacitor bank supplies exactly Qc = 864 VAR here, matching and canceling the load's inductive Q. The new apparent power becomes S' = P = 1152 VA, since Q is now zero, and at the same 120 V supply, the current drops from the original |I| = S/V = 1440/120 = 12 A down to |I'| = S'/V = 1152/120 = 9.6 A. That is a real, measurable 20 percent reduction in current for delivering the exact same 1152 W of useful power, which is why power factor correction is standard practice in any industrial facility running large motors, and why many utilities write power factor penalties directly into commercial and industrial electricity tariffs, turning this simple triangle into a line item on a real invoice.
